If we plug in $x=3$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{2}-6x+9}{16\sqrt{x+1}-4x-20} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{[{x}^{2}-6x+9]}^{′}}{[16\sqrt{x+1}-4x-20]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{2x-6}{(\frac{8}{\sqrt{x+1}}-4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x-3}{4(x+1)^{-1/2}-2}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{2}-6x+9}{16\sqrt{x+1}-4x-20} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x-3}{4(x+1)^{-1/2}-2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{[x-3]}^{′}}{{[4(x+1)^{-1/2}-2]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{1}{-2(x+1)^{-3/2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{x\to 3}(x+1)^{3/2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(3+1)^{3/2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8 \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$
